title: Chapter 71 — Defending the Book
intro: Protecting your existing trade accounts from competitor displacement and account erosion.

sections.title: Early Warning Signs
sections.content:
Account erosion is silent until it is sudden. Watch for: fewer quote requests than usual, longer response times from the account, questions about brands you do not carry, mentions of other suppliers' reps, and projects that should have come to you but went elsewhere.

Each signal alone might mean nothing. Three signals together mean someone is pitching your account. React immediately — do not wait for confirmation.

sections.title: Defence Strategies
sections.content:
Increase contact frequency. If you were calling monthly, start calling biweekly. Visit a job site. Invite them to an event. The competitor is adding touches — you need to match or exceed them.

Reinforce your value. 'I wanted to check in — your delivery track record with us this year has been 100 percent on time. I want to make sure we keep that going for your next project.' Remind them what they have without sounding desperate.

Address the competitor's pitch directly if you can: 'I heard [competitor] has been offering aggressive pricing on [category]. I want to make sure our pricing works for you. Can we review your tiers?'

Sometimes the best defence is offence — offer something new. A volume rebate. A priority delivery upgrade. An exclusive brand or product that the competitor cannot match.

sections.title: When You Lose
sections.content:
If you lose an account despite your best efforts, handle it professionally. 'I am disappointed but I respect your decision. If anything changes or if you need support on a project, I am still here.' Leave the door open.

Many lost accounts return within 12-18 months when the new supplier fails to deliver the same level of service. Be ready. The rescue is easier when you left on good terms.
